title: Shinran's family
hook: Shinran married and raised a family, neither monk nor layman

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shinran's sentence that sounds backward: even the good are born in the Pure Land, so how much more the bad.

A box of old letters, kept in a temple archive for a very long time, then read again. They are from a mother to her grown daughter. She writes about the man she married, how she first understood who he was, what she remembered of his hard years. The man was Shinran. The woman was his wife, Eshinni. A Buddhist monk with a wife, children, a household and letters home was not the usual picture in his world. Shinran found his own phrase for what he had become: neither monk nor layman. Today, Shinran's family.
screen: `A MOTHER'S LETTERS TO HER DAUGHTER.` → `SHINRAN AND ESHINNI.` → `NEITHER MONK NOR LAYMAN.`

segments.voice: First, how it happened. When the authorities moved against Honen's community, Shinran was among those sent into exile, and he was stripped of his status as a monk. He never went back to the monastery life. With his wife, Eshinni, he raised children, and lived among farmers and ordinary people in the provinces, teaching the nembutsu to whoever came. Second, his phrase. In the closing pages of his major work, the Kyogyoshinsho, he writes of himself that he is therefore neither monk nor layman. He took the name Gutoku, which carries the sense of a foolish, stubble-haired one: no longer a shaved monk, not quite a layman either. Third, the letters. Eshinni's letters to their daughter, Kakushinni, are among the ways Shinran can be seen as a person, not only as a teacher. They show a wife who respected him deeply and a family that lived through hard times together. Fourth, why it matters. Shinran's teaching put all the weight on Amida's vow, not on how pure a life a person could manage. A married man, raising children, working out the next meal, needed the vow as much as anyone, and could receive it as fully. In Jodo Shinshu, the school that grew from his teaching, temple priests may marry and raise families, and a temple can also be a family's home. Ordinary life, in this telling, is not a step down from the path. It is where the path is walked.
screen: `EXILED, AND NO LONGER A MONK.` · `NEITHER MONK NOR LAYMAN.` · `ESHINNI'S LETTERS.` · `ORDINARY LIFE IS WHERE IT'S WALKED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the most everyday part of your life, the dishes, the commute, the laundry, the people you live with or call, and choose one. Hold it in mind without wishing it were something grander, notice the care that is already in it, yours or someone else's, and let a breath or two be a quiet thank you to it.
Shinran's family. The teacher who married Eshinni, raised children, and called himself neither monk nor layman. Today's word.
